seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
In your sentence about Irishmen having no morals you seem to me to be accusing me of having acted immorally towards you in the matter of the Italian translation of the Ulysses episode. This is quite unjust on your part. When we were last dining together I told you about it and you asked me to write you a letter authorising you to get the episode from Rossi and print it in the Review you are interested in “l’Indice”. I sent you the letter the following day and after that heard nothing from you or Rossi or L’Indice or Il Convenio Convegno
which printed the episode without consulting me or paying me. Where does the immorality come in? If Il Convenio Convegno
immitates imitates the NRF as you say it might go a step farther and pay its contributors as the NRF does. The NRF paid me for the A.L.P. translation at the rate of Frcs.125 per page which is once and a half the present Fortnightly rates. I simply wanted your advice about the constant pilfering and publishing of my work in Italy without consulting me. I now have your advice that the case is hopeless. Thanks. You seem to me in this respect to have left the American frying pan for the Italian fire.

note.p: In a letter to Pound dated 13 February 1932, JJ complained that “Italian papers, Il Mattino (Naples), La Fiera Letteraria etc have several times published translations of things of mine. They never consult me, inform me or pay me. I see that Il Convegno last October or so published Rossi’s translation of Episode 1 of Ulysses. … Of course, they pay me nothing” (LIII 240). An Italian translation of the “Telemachus” episode of Ulysses by Alberto Rossi appeared in Il Convegno (Milan), vol. 12, no. 9-10 (October 1931): 476-502. Giacomo Prampolini published “Un Caso Penoso,” a translation of JJ’s short story “A Painful Case,” in La Fiera Letteraria (Milan), vol. 4, no. 23 (3 June 1928): 5. Slocum and Cahoon state that a translation of some work by JJ appeared in Il Mattino, a Neapolitan newspaper, sometime before 13 February 1932, but they are unable to identify it (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 121). JJ was not mollified when he was told that copyright in Dubliners, at least, had expired under Italian law (Robert Spoo, Without Copyrights: Piracy, Publishing, and the Public Domain [New York: Oxford University Press, 2013], 237, 319 n.23).

In a letter dated 15 February 1932, Pound blurted a response to JJ’s 13 February letter: “No Irishman has any morals.” He was suggesting that JJ’s complaints about unremunerative Italian translations of his writings seemed mercenary or materialistic. He added that a writer’s ability to live by his pen “conduces to independence and dissociation, rather than to coherence and cooperation” – possibly a glance at JJ’s patron-supported existence in Paris and his coterie-encouraged indulgence in what Pound viewed as the mistaken, solipsistic experiments of “Work in Progress,” later to be published as Finnegans Wake (see Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 564-65).

Pound may have felt that his remark, “No Irishman has any morals,” was stronger than he’d intended. In an undated letter that is clearly a reply to JJ’s present letter, he struggled to explain himself: “Yr interpretation of my interpretation of the term ‘morality’ is highly incorrect. I was considering things of the spirit, not LOW questions of commerce. Besides/ what evidence have we that the Irish OUGHT to be moral?” (The James Joyce-Paul Léon Papers in the National Library of Ireland: A Catalogue, comp. Catherine Fahy [Dublin: National Library of Ireland, 1992], 114). This confused justification no doubt failed to placate JJ and only served to dig Pound’s hole deeper.

Pound frequently contributed to the Genoa journal L’Indice during the early 1930s on subjects ranging from JJ and Jean Cocteau to Leo Frobenius. He told Wyndham Lewis that L’Indice was “most active fortnightly or other rev. in Italy” (Pound/Lewis: The Letters of Ezra Pound and Wyndham Lewis, ed. Timothy Materer [New York: New Directions, 1985], 170). Evidently, Pound had promised to assist JJ in getting the Alberto Rossi translation of “Telemachus” published in L’Indice (not Il Convegno where it appeared without JJ’s knowledge). Pound wrote JJ on 15 February 1932: “By abusing my own good nature and being the usual g;d; fool I wasted time answering Rossi’s questions, in which R. displayed a fairly comprehensive ignorance of modern irish. At any rate as the stuff was sent to some rival nooz stand [Il Convegno] and not to l’Indice I don’t see that I can be expected to take any further action about it” (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 564-65).

In an undated postcard evidently mailed to JJ soon after Pound’s 15 February 1932 letter, Pound added that he had just seen Alberto Rossi in person: “VERY simpatico and apparently intelligent. He has never heard of the Convegno paying anyone. He certainly has not been pd/ for translation. … At any rate having seen him, my opinion has riz. I shdnt. have spoke hard of him” (ibid., 566-67). In another letter around this time, Pound informed the “[d]ear but eternally naive Jhamez” that Il Convegno “is by the way one of my particular abominations,” and that “there is NO cash in these transactions [Italian magazine translations of foreign authors]” (The James Joyce-Paul Léon Papers in the National Library of Ireland, 114).

In addition to “Telemachus,” Alberto Rossi translated “Proteus” and Pomes Penyeach (Poesia da un soldo; Dall’“Ulisse” [Milan: Enrico Cederna, 1949]) and wrote the preface for an Italian translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1933). Serenella Zanotti has shown that Pound helped Rossi with his translations of JJ’s writings (“Pound, Linati, and the Early Italian Translations of Ulysses,” in Joyce and/in Translation, ed. Rosa Maria Bollettieri Bosinelli and Ira Torresi [Rome: Bulzoni, 2007], 53-75). Rossi published an obituary of JJ in the Gazzetta del Popolo for 14 January 1941. For details regarding Rossi’s translations of JJ and other Italian versions of works by JJ, see Slocum and Cahoon (119-22).

div.note: Il Convegno was a review founded in Milan in 1920 by the theater director and critic, Enzo Ferrieri (1896-1969). In the 1920s, the review published Carlo Linati’s translations of JJ’s play Exiles (Esuli), his short story “Araby,” and part of Ulysses (Slocum and Cahoon, 120-21).

Pound had written in his letter to JJ of 15 February 1932: “As for Convegno, Ferrieri’s gt/ ambish/ iz that Convegno shd/ serve as carta igenica [toilet paper] to the N;r.f. [Nouvelle Revue Française] / / at any rate I am not to be found in that gabinetto [water closet]” (Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” 564).

La Nouvelle Revue Française was founded in 1909 by André Gide, Jean Schlumberger, and Jacques Copeau, and published many important French writers, as well as French translations of the “Proteus” (“Protée”) episode of Ulysses, by Auguste Morel and Stuart Gilbert, vol. 15, no. 179 (1 August 1928): 204-226, and of Anna Livia Plurabelle (published as “Anna Livie Plurabelle”), by Samuel Beckett, Eugène Jolas, and others, vol. 19, no. 212 (1 May 1931): 633-46.

The Fortnightly Review was a highly influential British magazine, founded in 1865 by Anthony Trollope and several others. The magazine published JJ’s early article, “Ibsen’s New Drama,” n.s., vol. 67, no. 400 (1 April 1900): 575-90, for which JJ was paid twelve guineas (Ellmann, JJ 74). Pound published early poems and essays in The Fortnightly Review, including pieces on Vorticism (1914) and Remy de Gourmont (1915).

JJ may be suggesting that Pound, having refused to sign the international protest against Samuel Roth’s unauthorized serialization of Ulysses in America several years before, is now showing a similar indifference to unauthorized Italian translations of JJ’s works (see JJ to Pound, 16 November 1926, notes).
